source: Year 12 Economics Booklet 2027, topic glossaries, pages 21 to 37, with additions and revisions made on 13 November 2026

terms.def: A country has an absolute advantage when it can produce a good using fewer resources than another country. Absolute advantage alone does not explain why trade benefits both countries; comparative advantage does.

Accrual budgeting represents international best practice in public sector financial management and reporting. The main advantage of accrual measures (as opposed to cash) is that they provide a more comprehensive indication of the total activity of government and the long-term effects of current policy.

High-income economies with diversified industry structures, large service sectors, developed financial systems and high living standards, such as Australia, the United States, Japan and most of Western Europe.

The total demand for goods and services generated by the sum of all spending in the economy. A basic proposition of economic analysis is that the level of production, employment, and income are determined by the level of total spending on final goods and services. Y=C+I+G+X-M

The total quantity of goods and services that firms in an economy are willing and able to produce at each price level. Aggregate supply increases with improvements in productivity, technology and the quantity of resources.
Resources are used to produce the goods and services that consumers value most.
Behaviour that reduces the level of competition in the market.
APEC is the Asia - Pacific Economic Co-operation Forum. It was mainly formed in response to the development of trading blocs such as the EU. It aims to promote co-operation among nations.
A rise in the free-market exchange rate of the domestic currency with foreign currencies.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations is an organisation of nations from that region, which has agreed to free trade among member countries.

AUSFTA is a preferential trade agreement between Australia and the USA which began in 2005. It is not a completely ‘free trade’ agreement as there are still many restrictions especially in agriculture.

An independent Commonwealth statutory authority that enforces the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (formerly the Trade Practices Act 1974). The ACCC promotes competition and fair trading, assesses mergers, protects consumers and regulates national infrastructure services.

A mechanism that decreases the size of fluctuations in the level of spending in the economy. For example when the economy expands, government spending on welfare is reduced and tax revenue will increase. Import expenditure and savings also follow this pattern as automatic stabilisers.
These are minimum wages and working conditions legislated by the government or an industrial tribunal (see Fair Pay Commission).
A complete statement of all transactions between one country and the rest of the world in any specific period.

The value of exports of goods and services minus the value of imports of goods and services. It is part of the current account and reflects Australia's international competitiveness and terms of trade.

A bank bill generally arises from a short-term credit arrangement designed to enable businesses to obtain funds to finance commercial transactions. The bills are accepted by the bank that endorses them.
The test applied by the Fair Work Commission when approving an enterprise agreement: each employee must be better off overall under the agreement than under the relevant modern award.
A trading agreement between 2 countries eg ANZCER,
The market for existing government securities.
When inflation or wage growth pushes income earners into higher tax brackets, raising their average tax rate without a change in tax law. Also called fiscal drag.
The budget result. The difference between revenue and expenses. It is also known as the fiscal balance.

Whether the budget is expansionary or contractionary. It is judged by the change in the budget outcome, especially its structural component, rather than by whether the budget is in deficit or surplus.
Fluctuations in the level of economic activity over time, moving through expansion, peak, contraction (or recession) and trough.
The record of all financial transactions involving Australian claims on and liabilities to foreigners.
The sudden withdrawal of funds from a country.
A tax levied on increases in value of a capital asset, such as shares or real estate.

The equilibrium interest rate in the market for exchange settlement funds, also referred to as the money market. The cash rate is targeted by the Reserve Bank through market operations. It is the interest rate on unsecured overnight loans between banks

A bank whose functions are: To have sole control over the issue of currency and usually also to control the nation's reserves of gold and foreign exchange; To act as banker to the central government and to the banking system; To advise and assist the central government on financial and monetary matters; To implement officially determined monetary policy by regulating the monetary and banking system.

CERTA is a bilateral (between 2 countries) trading agreement, between Australia and New Zealand. The Closer Economic Relations Trading Agreement has led to the elimination of tariffs and other quantitative restrictions on trade between Australia and NZ.
A model of the economy showing the flows of income and spending between households, firms, the financial sector, government and the overseas sector.
The world prices of raw materials such as iron ore, coal, gas and wheat. They strongly influence Australia's terms of trade and the value of the dollar.

A Commonwealth government security is originally issued as a means to finance a budget deficit. It is a form of borrowing where by the Australian Government agrees to pay the holder a fixed some of money over a period of time and pays the face value of the security on maturity. They include treasury notes and government bonds.

A country has a comparative advantage when it can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than other countries. Specialising according to comparative advantage and trading raises total world output and allows both trading partners to gain.
The Commonwealth law, enforced by the ACCC, that prohibits anti-competitive conduct and protects consumers. It replaced the Trade Practices Act 1974 in 2011.
Government policies that promote competition between firms and prevent anti- competitive conduct, such as the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and the work of the ACCC.
The types of goods and services that a country exports and imports, for example resources, manufactures, rural goods and services.
Fiscal or monetary policy that reduces aggregate demand to slow economic growth and reduce inflationary pressure, for example raising the cash rate or reducing a budget deficit.
A government business enterprise that remains in government ownership, but its management structure is altered so that it operates like a privately owned enterprise.
Inflation caused by increases in the costs of production, such as wages, energy and raw materials, which firms pass on to consumers as higher prices.
Policy that works against the business cycle: stimulating demand in a downturn and restraining it in a boom.
In Australia, inflation is measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI). This is the price of a basket of the normal goods and services people buy in Australia.
The lending of money to another party. It involves an agreement to repay the temporary loan.
When government borrowing to finance a budget deficit raises interest rates and so reduces private sector investment and consumption.

A record of receipts from the sale of goods and services to foreigners, the payments for goods and services bought from foreigners, and property income (such as interest and profits) and current transfers (such as gifts) received from and paid to foreigners.

When debits on the current account exceed credits, so Australia pays more to the rest of the world for goods, services and income than it receives. A CAD must be financed by a surplus on the capital and financial account.
The changes in the budget outcome as a result of changes in the level of economic activity.
Unemployment arising from a slowdown in the pace of economic expansion or aggregate demand.
Whatever is owed, be it money, goods, or services, by one person or organisation to another.
The proportion of export earnings needed to pay interest on net foreign debt. It indicates the burden of foreign debt on the economy.
A system where wages and conditions are set by bargaining at the level of the enterprise or the individual, not by a central tribunal for whole industries.
Estimates of expenses are greater than estimates of revenue.
A sustained fall in the general level of prices.
Inflation caused by aggregate demand growing faster than the economy's capacity to supply goods and services, so prices are bid up.
A fall in the free-market exchange rate of the domestic currency with foreign currencies.
The removal or reduction of government rules and restrictions on a market, aimed at increasing competition and efficiency.

Derivates are simple financial contracts whose value is linked to or derived from an underlying asset, such as stocks, bonds, commodities, loans and exchange rates. They are international financial instruments for spreading risk or hedging. They include: futures, options, swaps, forward rate agreements and other hedging instruments.

Low- and lower-middle-income economies with relatively low GDP per capita, a large share of employment in agriculture, lower levels of health and education, and greater vulnerability to external shocks.

Economic Development is the physical situation and the state of mind whereby a society through some combination of social, economic and institutional processes secures the means to obtain a better life.
Equity investment in Australia by non-residents.
The countries or regions a nation trades with. For Australia, Asian economies, and China in particular, are the major destinations for exports.
A floating exchange rate in which the central bank occasionally intervenes in the foreign exchange market to smooth large swings in the currency's value. Also called a managed float.
Deliberate changes in government spending and taxation decided in the budget to influence the level of economic activity.
A fall in the rate of inflation: prices are still rising, but more slowly.
Selling goods in an export market at a price below their cost of production or below the price charged in the home market. Dumping is a common justification for anti-dumping duties.
The ability of firms and the economy to adapt to change and innovate over time.
This is a process where industrial development is accompanied by preservation of the environment.
A broad measure of welfare that covers not only income per person but also health, education, the distribution of income and the quality of the environment.

An increase in the volume of goods and services produced in an economy over a period of time, measured by the percentage change in real GDP. Growth is a quantitative measure and is not the same as economic development.
The effective rate of protection of an industry is defined as the percentage by which all of a nation’s trade barriers raised the industry’s value added, per unit of output.
These are economies than are in transition from low to middle income economies to high income economies as a result of opening their markets and high levels of economic growth.
A market-based policy that caps total emissions and lets firms buy and sell permits to emit, putting a price on carbon.
An agreement reached through enterprise bargaining that states the working conditions in that enterprise, industry or business.
The process of negotiation between employers and employees (and or unions) in regard to industrial relations issues, such as wages and conditions.
The share market. The rights (shares) to partial ownership of companies are bought and sold.

The EU was formed out of the European Community (EC) in 1993. It had 27 member countries, including Britain, Germany and France. There are free trade, capital and labour movements among member countries. Thirteen EU members adopt the EURO as a common currency. They make-up the Euro Area.
The price of one currency in terms of another, such as the number of US dollars needed to buy one Australian dollar.
Accounts held by banks at the Reserve Bank and used to settle payments between banks. The RBA's market operations change the funds in these accounts to keep the cash rate at its target.
Fiscal or monetary policy that increases aggregate demand to stimulate growth and reduce unemployment, for example cutting the cash rate or increasing government spending.
Government assistance such as grants, tax concessions or cheap finance that lowers the cost of exporting and makes domestic producers more competitive in world markets. A form of protection.
Export propensity measures the proportion of goods produced domestically that are exported.
An economy's ability to meet its financial obligations to the rest of the world in the long run, judged by the current account, foreign liabilities and the exchange rate.
Costs or benefits of production or consumption that affect society, but not necessarily the producers or consumers of the product.
Sets out the conditions of workplace relations in Australia.
The name of the national workplace relations tribunal from 2009 until 1 January 2013, when it was renamed the Fair Work Commission. See Fair Work Commission.

Australia's national workplace relations tribunal. It sets the national minimum wage in its Annual Wage Review, maintains modern awards, approves enterprise agreements and resolves workplace disputes.
The record of all transactions in financial assets and liabilities between Australians and foreigners.
The development of new financial products and methods of borrowing and lending.
An organisation that takes money from households or firms and lends it to other households or firms.
The fiscal balance is the accrual equivalent of the underlying cash balance. A fiscal surplus indicates that the Government is saving more than enough to finance all of its investment spending.
A deliberate reduction in a budget deficit, through lower spending or higher taxes, to stabilise or reduce government debt.
The use of the Commonwealth budget — government spending and taxation — to influence the level of economic activity and achieve the government's economic objectives.
An exchange rate that is pegged by the country's central bank.
An exchange rate determined by the forces of demand and supply in the foreign exchange market, with little or no government intervention. The Australian dollar has floated since December 1983.

A foreign exchange swap is similar to a repurchase agreement, except they involve the exchange of cash for foreign currency. To increase liquidity the Reserve Bank will swap Australian currency for foreign currency. This will increase the supply of Australian currency in the money market. The foreign currency swap will then be reversed at a set time and a set price in the future. The opposite happens if the Reserve Bank wants to reduce liquidity.

There are two measurements of the Foreign or External Debt. They are:- Gross Foreign Debt, i.e. the total borrowings by Australian residents from non-residents. Net Foreign Debt, i.e. the Gross Debt minus Australia’s holdings of foreign reserves, and gold, and lending Australian residents have made overseas.

Investment that gives the investor a lasting interest in, and a significant degree of influence over, an enterprise in another economy, usually defined as owning 10 per cent or more of the enterprise.
The market in which the currencies of different countries are exchanged for one another. It is also known as the FOREX market.
Someone who consumes a product without paying for it.
International trade without government-imposed barriers such as tariffs, quotas or subsidies. Free trade allows countries to specialise according to comparative advantage.
An agreement between two or more countries to reduce or remove barriers to trade between them. Also called a preferential trade agreement.
Unemployment arising from new entrants into the labour market and those workers waiting to start a new job.

A tax on businesses for payments, usually in kind, made to employees over and above wages and salaries. Fringe benefits such as a company car, or an expense account, or payment of superannuation premiums are provided in order to attract and hold staff, and for motivation purpose.
The level of unemployment at which there is no cyclical unemployment and inflation is stable. See NAIRU.
The market where agreements are made, that commodities and other products will be bought or sold at a later date, at a fixed price, determined at the time that the contract is agreed to.

The Group of Twenty (G20) Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors. This was established in 1999 to bring together important industrialised and developing economies to discuss key issues in the global economy. The G20 is made up of 19 of the main countries in the world plus the European Union. Australia is a member of the G20.

The Group of Seven (G7) is a forum of the leaders of seven major advanced economies: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States. The European Union also takes part. It began in 1975 as a group of six and became the G7 when Canada joined in 1976. Russia joined in 1997, making it the Group of Eight (G8), but was suspended in 2014 after its annexation of Crimea, so the group is the G7 again. The leaders meet at an annual summit to discuss and co-ordinate international policies.

The area between the Lorenz curve and the 45 degree line divided by the total area under the 45 degree line. It is a measurement of income equality. The larger the gini coefficient the larger is the level of income inequality.

The Global economy is the world economy. It is the economic activity going on in the world. It includes all production, trade, financial flows, investment, technology, labour and economic behaviour in nations and between nations.
The spreading of the stages of production of a good across several countries, each stage located where it can be done most cheaply or efficiently. Also called a global supply chain.

Globalisation is the actual movement, the capacity to move and the potential movement across nations of trade, investment, technology, finance and labour. It also involves the effects of these forces.
A tax on goods and services. It is a regressive tax.
The plan of expected expenses and revenue of the government, usually for the next fiscal year.
Businesses owned by the government.
The total income earned by a country's residents, including net income from overseas, divided by the population. The World Bank uses GNI per capita to classify economies by income level.
This is the value of the world’s output, also known as World Real GDP. It is the aggregate of individual nation’s outputs.

People who have been out of work for a long time and find it very hard to get and keep a job because of personal barriers, such as poor health, disability or a lack of basic skills. They are unlikely to be hired even when jobs are available.
This is the actual change in the size of government expenses and revenue, including changes in assets and liabilities. A larger headline surplus allows debt repayment.
The percentage change in the Consumer Price Index over a period, including all items in the basket, even prices that are volatile or affected by one-off changes.
Unemployment represented by discouraged workers and not included in published unemployment statistics.
Human capital is the value of a person’s education, skills and experience.

The HDI is part of the Human Development Report. It is a measure of human development that includes, measurements that reflect: a long and healthy life, access to knowledge and a decent standard of living.

The impact of a tax refers to the point at which it is imposed initially. In the case of an excise duty, the impact of the tax is on the manufacturer; the incidence of the tax, however, may be on the final consumer.
A type of price index. As an example, the implicit price deflator for Gross Domestic Product is calculated by comparing movements in GPD in current prices and constant prices.
Import penetration measures the proportion of goods sold domestically that are imported.
Inflation caused by rising prices of imported goods and services, for example because of a depreciation of the exchange rate or higher world prices.
The final resting place of a tax is called the incident of the tax.
Income is the flow of earnings received by an individual and includes sources such as wages, salaries, commissions, dividends, interest and rent.
The tax on income or the part of income liable to tax. It is determined by deducting from accessible income (gross income) all allowable deductions.
These are taxes paid on goods and services that have been purchased. The tax is included in the purchase price.
A dispute or disagreement in the work place that causes a stoppage of work. These disputes often relate to managerial policy, wages, physical working conditions and hours of work.

Industrial relations commissions or tribunals are agencies that historically have been set up by the federal or state governments to consider issues such as industrial dispute resolution, award determination and enterprise agreement registration. At the national level this role is now carried out by the Fair Work Commission; some states still have their own industrial relations commission.
The argument that a new domestic industry should be protected until it grows large enough to achieve economies of scale and compete with established foreign producers.
A sustained increase in the general level of prices, measured in Australia by the Consumer Price Index.
The framework under which the RBA sets the cash rate to keep consumer price inflation between 2 and 3 per cent, on average, over time.

An expectation of the inflationary cycle based on the argument that once high rates of inflation come to be expected, inflation will be maintained over a period of time. Inflation becomes built into the system.
Injections equal investment plus government expenditure plus expenditure on exports.
The principle that the present generation should meet its needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It underlies ecologically sustainable development.

The fluctuations in the level of economic activity in the world economy over time, moving through phases of expansion, peak, contraction and trough. Changes in major economies spread to others through trade and financial flows.
The price and non-price advantages an industry or country has over foreign competitors.
The way the stages of producing goods and services are spread across countries, with each stage located where it can be done most efficiently.

The IMF is the International Monetary Fund. It was set up along with the World Bank after World War II to aid and stabilise International Capital Markets. The IMF was responsible for monitoring and stabilising the international financial system through the short - term financing of balance of payments deficits.
The effect of a currency devaluation on the balance of goods and services. It generally applies in a fixed exchange rate system.

An inverted-U curve suggesting that income inequality first rises and then falls as an economy develops and per capita income increases. The environmental Kuznets curve applies the same idea to pollution.

An international treaty on climate change, adopted in 1997 and in force from 2005, that set binding targets for developed countries to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. Australia ratified it in 2007. It has been superseded by the Paris Agreement (2015), under which every country sets its own emissions target.

The total number of available workers in an economy, at a particular time. The labour force may be classified according to those in various types of employment and those unemployed, but actively seeking work. Also known as the workforce.
The labour force underutilisation rate represents the underutilisation of labour within the labour force and is the sum of the unemployment and underemployment rates.
Policies that effect the operation of the labour market.
The degree to which an asset can be instantly converted into cash at a known price.
Regulations requiring a minimum proportion of a product to be produced or sourced domestically. They protect local producers but raise costs for firms and consumers.
The long-term unemployed are the unemployed that have been out of work for more than 12 months.
A curve showing the proportion of national income earned by a particular percentage of the population (measured from the poorest upwards).
Policies that influence the overall level of demand in the economy: fiscal policy and monetary policy.
Actions of the central bank to intervene in the foreign exchange market to influence the value of the currency.
The proportion of each additional dollar of income that is spent on consumption. The higher the MPC, the larger the multiplier.
The proportion of each additional dollar of income that is saved. MPC plus MPS equals 1.
The extra tax paid as a proportion of the change in income received. It is calculated by dividing the change in tax by the change in income.
A situation in which the market mechanism does not allocate resources efficiently, for example because of externalities, public goods or a lack of competition.
Reserve Bank activity in the money market, in implementing monetary policy, through targeting the cash rate.
The attempt to increase output from given inputs of labour, capital, and materials by increasing efficiency.
The ease with which labour can be transferred from one occupation to another or from one geographical location to another.
Industry or occupation-based minimum pay and conditions set by the Fair Work Commission. They form the safety net with the National Employment Standards.
The attempt to control inflation and promote economic stability and to moderate the business cycle by changing the quantity of money in circulation and adjusting interest rates.
A group of countries that share a single currency and a common monetary policy set by one central bank, such as the euro area and the European Central Bank.
This is a trading agreement between many nations at one time such as through the WTO or APEC.
An initial change in aggregate demand leads to an eventual change in national income that is greater than the initial change. It is equal to 1 divided by 1- MPC.

The North American Free Trade Agreement was a free trade agreement between Canada, the USA and Mexico that began in 1994. It was replaced by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) on 1 July 2020. See USMCA.

The NAIRU is the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment, also referred to as the natural rate of unemployment. It is the level of unemployment that can be sustained at a set period of time without having major inflationary effects.
The national or public debt is the net liabilities of Australian governments.
The lowest hourly rate that can legally be paid to an adult employee not covered by an award or agreement, set each year by the Fair Work Commission.
The natural rate of unemployment, often referred to as the NAIRU (non- accelerating inflation rate of unemployment), is the long run rate of unemployment a nation can sustain.
A cost of production or consumption that falls on third parties and is not reflected in the market price, such as pollution.
The total amount Australians owe to foreigners in borrowed funds, minus the amount foreigners owe to Australians.
The value of foreign ownership of Australian assets, such as shares and property, minus Australian ownership of foreign assets.
A nation’s total foreign liabilities (financial obligations) minus total foreign assets.
Income earned by Australian residents from overseas (interest, dividends and wages) minus income paid to non-residents. It is usually the largest deficit item on the current account.
A balance between the greenhouse gases emitted and those removed from the atmosphere. Australia has a legislated target of net zero by 2050.
The numerical value of the actual rate of protection listed by a country. It generally relates to the level of a tariff.
Benefits from working that are not related to wages, such as superannuation, sick leave and holidays.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development: a forum of mostly advanced economies that researches and promotes policies for economic growth and living standards.
Relocating part of a firm's production or services to another country, usually to reduce costs, while the firm keeps ownership of the operation.
The relationship between economic growth and unemployment: growth must exceed a certain rate (roughly 3 per cent in Australia) before the unemployment rate begins to fall.
The difference between actual output and the economy's potential output. A negative gap means spare capacity; a positive gap adds to inflation.
Contracting another firm to perform a task previously done within the business. When the contractor is overseas, it is international outsourcing.
The 2015 international treaty in which countries set their own emissions targets to limit global warming to well below 2°C. It succeeded the Kyoto Protocol.
Work less than a normal working week. This is often considered to be less than 35 hours a week.
The proportion of the working age population, 15-65 years old, recorded as either in work or looking for work.
Shows the relationship between the inflation rate and the unemployment rate.

The PQLI was developed as an alternative and improved measurement of living standards, at the end of the 1970’s. The index included three basic indicators: • Life expectancy at age1. • Infant mortality. • Literacy.
The argument that a current account deficit caused by private sector borrowing for productive investment need not be a concern, because private borrowers weigh up the risks and returns themselves.
The combination of macroeconomic (fiscal and monetary) and microeconomic policies used together to achieve the government's economic objectives.
Limits on economic policy that come from the need to win public and parliamentary support, which can delay or weaken reforms.
Purchases by companies and individuals of shares and debentures issued by Australian and overseas companies.
Policies designed to influence the level of prices and incomes. The most common ones are wages policies.
Net primary income is the difference between income received from overseas and income paid overseas, such as royalties, dividends, and interest on money owed (foreign debt)
Goods that someone or a group owns. Some people are excluded from using it usually as a result of price.
The process of selling a public corporation to private shareholders.
The quantity of output produced per unit of input, most commonly output per hour worked (labour productivity). Productivity growth is the main source of rising living standards over time.
A tax whose rate (marginal tax rate) increases as the amount of taxable income increases, eg personal income tax.
A tax whose rate (marginal tax rate) remains the same regardless of the amount of taxable income.
Government action that gives domestic producers an advantage over foreign competitors, such as tariffs, subsidies, quotas, local content rules and export incentives.
Goods or services that can be consumed by everyone and from which no one can be excluded, e.g. defense.
That sector of the economy, which is owned and directly controlled by the government. It includes both government and semi-government bodies.

This measure compares the relative prices of products in different countries. The relative value of each county's currency depends on the quantity of goods and services that can be purchased with it. PPP can be measured in absolute terms or relative terms.
The general living standard a person has.
A central bank buying government bonds and other assets to lower long-term interest rates when the cash rate is already near zero.
A limit on the quantity or value of a good that can be imported in a period. A quota reduces supply in the domestic market, raising prices and protecting domestic producers.
The board of the Reserve Bank, formed in March 2025, that decides the cash rate target. It meets eight times a year and announces its decision at 2.30 pm on the second day of each meeting.
Gross Domestic Product adjusted for inflation, so that changes reflect changes in the volume of output rather than in prices. Also called GDP at constant prices.
The nominal interest rate adjusted to compensate for inflation.
Wages adjusted for inflation, showing the change in what wages can actually buy.
A period of falling economic activity, commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative growth in real GDP.
The fluctuations in economic activity shared by the economies of a region, such as East Asia, because of their close trade and financial links.
A tax, which takes a smaller proportion of income as taxable income increases.

This is calculated as a proportion of average earnings. People living below this level are said to be in relative poverty, in comparison to the other people in that nation. They lack the basic necessities in relation to the general standard of living in a country.

A repurchase agreement is an agreement, between the Reserve Bank and a bank, that the Reserve Bank buys or sells a security on the understanding that the dealers agree to repurchase or sell the security at a specified date and at an agreed price. It is used to cover temporary fluctuations in the supply of cash. This is the most common form of transaction in the cash market.

Australia's Central Bank. The Reserve Bank is responsible for maintaining the stability of the financial system. Financial stability is an essential ingredient in maintaining macro-economic stability and the confidence of the community in undertaking their financial transactions. Within this broad mandate, the Bank also has specific responsibility for the safety and efficiency of the payments system, a responsibility overseen by the Payments System Board
An increase (revaluation) or decrease (devaluation) in the value of a currency under a fixed exchange rate system, decided by the government or central bank.
The Australian Government scheme that sets declining emissions limits (baselines) for the country's largest industrial facilities.
A minimum guaranteed standard of wages and working conditions.
Unemployment occurring in industries or regions where the demand for labour is lower at certain times of the year.
This involves money transfers between countries, e.g. foreign aid, and sending money to relatives overseas.
The market for equities. Shares are bought and sold, which gives claim to the partial ownership of a company.

Costs which do not appear in the account of a firm; eg. the cost to the community and individual of noise, air pollution and traffic congestion. The cost is borne by non-producers and non-consumers of the product.
Government-provided benefits in cash or in kind, such as Medicare, public education and welfare payments, that add to household living standards.
Government debt, also known as public debt or national debt. It usually relates to bonds or debt that are in a foreign currency.
Buying or selling a financial asset, such as a currency, in the hope of profiting from a change in its price.
Rising inflation at the same time as weak growth and rising unemployment, usually after a negative supply shock.
The larger and more lasting adjustments which occur in the structure of production in the economy; for example, changes in the relative size and characteristics of industries.
The budget outcome if the economy was at full employment. This relates to the effects of changes in policy on the budget outcome, as distinct from changes in the level of GDP (cyclical component).
Unemployment that arises from changes in the pattern of demand or supply in the economy.
A government payment to domestic producers that lowers their costs of production, allowing them to compete with imports or sell more cheaply in export markets.
An excess of government revenue over government expenses. T is greater than G.
The 17 goals adopted by United Nations members in 2015 to end poverty, protect the environment and improve living standards by 2030.
A tax on imported goods. A tariff raises the domestic price of imports, protects local producers from competition and raises revenue for the government.
The taxation system should not cause inefficient resource allocation.
The starting point where the tax is charged. This is generally the income level that is first subject to the tax.
Producing the maximum output from a given quantity of inputs, or a given output at the lowest cost. Also called productive efficiency.
The spread of new technologies and production methods across firms and countries, often through trade, foreign investment and the activities of transnational corporations.

The terms of trade is the ratio of a nation's export price to their import price. When the terms of trade improves (increased export prices relative to import prices) a nation is better off, as it can buy more imports with the same level of exports. A worsening of the terms of trade means a nation must sell more exports to purchase the same quantity of imports.
The time it takes for something to have an effect.
The removal or reduction of barriers to trade, such as tariffs and quotas, so that goods and services move more freely between countries.
Policies that are designed to effect trade. They may favour free trade or be protectionist.

The Trade Practices Act 1974 was Australia's main competition and consumer protection law until 1 January 2011, when it was replaced by the Competition and Consumer Act 2010. It covered anti-competitive and unfair market practices, mergers and acquisitions of companies, product safety and liability, and third-party access to facilities of national significance.

A weighted average exchange rate expressed as an index, where the value of the index is 100 in a specific base year. This is the main measurement of Australia's exchange rate compared to its main trading partners.
A group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers among members while keeping barriers against non-members, such as ASEAN or the European Union.
Payments from government to individuals for which no good or service is received in return, such as the Age Pension and JobSeeker.

The channels through which a change in the cash rate affects the economy: other interest rates, cash flows, asset prices and wealth, and the exchange rate, then aggregate demand, output and inflation.
A TNC is a company that operates in more than one country. It generally has subsidiaries or branches in a number of countries.
The RBA's preferred measure of underlying inflation. It removes the 15% of items with the largest price rises and the 15% with the smallest.
Workers who have a job but want, and are available for, more hours than they currently work.
This the most accurate measure of the government's budget funding requirements in a particular year. Over the long term it will equal the fiscal balance.
A measure of inflation that removes volatile price movements to show the persistent trend. The RBA mainly uses the trimmed mean, which excludes the largest price rises and falls each period.
The number of workers who are part of the labour force and are not employed but are actively seeking employment.
Unemployment expressed as a percentage of the labour force.
The global organisation of 193 member states that promotes peace, development and co-operation, including through the Sustainable Development Goals.

The Agreement between the United States of America, the United Mexican States, and Canada is a free trade agreement among the United States, Mexico, and Canada, in effect from July 1, 2020. It replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement implemented in 1994.
The change in the Australian-dollar value of foreign debt and assets caused by a movement in the exchange rate, with no new borrowing or lending.
The effects of a currency depreciation followed by an appreciation in a floating exchange rate system.
The ABS measure of the change in hourly rates of pay, used as the main indicator of wages growth.
Wealth is the stock of assets owned by an individual and includes items such as shares, bank deposits, superannuation, houses and land.
Incomes of households or firms that are not directly put back into spending. Withdrawals equal net savings plus net taxes plus import expenditure.
The World Bank is an international financial institution. The main function of the World Bank is to promote growth and prosperity by providing long-term loans for investment.
The main group promoting free trade in the world economy. It grew out of GATT in the 1990's.
